name: Adam Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Adam. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. To start, could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm cell lead on the day shift at Halden Hydraulics. We machine valve bodies, these heavy blocks of aluminium and steel with oil channels drilled through them, for tractors and diggers. I've got four CNC machines in my cell, which are computer-controlled lathes and mills, and three operators. I start at six, check the tool wear from the night, load the first fixtures, and then my day is measuring parts, swapping cutting tools and calling Viktor in the office when a program does something stupid.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like holding a finished part that's right to two hundredths of a millimetre. There's a gauge we use, and when the whole batch passes I feel ten feet tall. What wears me out is that I'm doing half of Viktor's job for operator money. I'm one of the best in the building and I still borrowed from my brother last March to cover the deposit on our flat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sometimes. I used one to translate a German manual for a new spindle, and once to help write my shift report when I was tired. I don't trust it for anything that matters yet. I wait until I've seen it work for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the hype dies down. Honestly, that's what Viktor keeps saying will happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was a useful tool and not much more. At work we'd joke about it, because the boss spent a fortune on that AI quality camera that still flags shadows as cracks. Online I'd probably not say anything, I mostly read football forums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the fight goes back to the normal fight. Pay, hours, whether Halden ever moves the work to a cheaper country. That was always the bigger threat to us than AI, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working, and I'd ask the union rep to push for a pay grade for cell leads, because there isn't one. I'd pay my brother back the rest, about three hundred, before the end of the year. And I'd keep using the translation tool, because that part does work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, a bit bored, like nothing happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the work moving to a cheaper country. Has that come up at Halden?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twice. In 2023 they moved the small valve line to a plant abroad and twenty people went. Every year since, someone in the canteen says we're next. So AI being hype doesn't make me feel safe, it just leaves the old worry where it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lina say about the pay grade idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say ask for it in writing this time. Last time my manager said he'd look into it and then he went on holiday for three weeks. She works as a teaching assistant, she's used to people promising things to children and not doing them.

S0.say: Fair enough, it was a useful tool and not much more. The boss's AI quality camera still flags shadows as cracks.
S0.think: The fight goes back to the normal fight about pay, hours and whether the work moves abroad. That was always the bigger threat than AI.
S0.do: Keeps working as before and asks the union rep to push for a proper pay grade for cell leads. Pays his brother back the remaining 300 by the end of the year and keeps using AI for translating manuals.
S0.feel: Calm, a little relieved and a little bored.
S0.quote: The boss spent a fortune on that AI quality camera that still flags shadows as cracks.
S0.fieldNote: Adam's real fear in the calm picture is offshoring, which already cost 20 jobs at Halden in 2023. He's pragmatic about AI: he uses it where it's proven, like translation, and nowhere else. The unpaid extra work he does for the programmer is a running grievance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels more real to me. You can already see it starting in the machine shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but workers need a seat at the table. If machines take tasks, the people who knew those tasks should be first in line for the new jobs, with training paid by the company. I'd say it at union meetings and I'd say it to my manager, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be okay, if I move. Loading fixtures and swapping tools, that's going to robots, Halden already has quotes for a robot loader. But someone has to program the cells and keep them running, and I already do half of that. The ones I worry about are my three operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen the robot loader actually working in our cell, not in a sales video, I'd ask Halden to pay for the CNC programming course at the technical college. It's two evenings a week for a year. I'd push the union to make that course part of the automation deal for everyone. And I'd start using AI properly to help me learn the programming code, because Viktor says that's how the young engineers do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but also, there's a part of me that's excited. I've wanted to get off the shop floor money for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see the robot loader working first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen three salesmen walk through our shop with tablets and promises. The quality camera was going to save two jobs and it created one, the guy who checks the camera. When the loader runs a full night shift with no one babysitting it, then I'll believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your three operators. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to sign up for the course with me, especially Jonas, he's sharp. But Rui is fifty-six and he's told me straight he's not going back to school. I don't know what I'd say to Rui. Maybe that the union will fight for him to stay on as a setter.

S1.say: Workers need a seat at the table. The people who knew the old tasks should be first in line for the new jobs, with company-paid training.
S1.think: I'd be okay if I move into programming, because I already do half of it. Loading and tool changes will go to robots, and my three operators are the ones at risk.
S1.do: Waits until the robot loader has proved itself in his own cell, then asks Halden to fund a year-long CNC programming course, two evenings a week. Pushes the union to include the course in the automation deal and uses AI tools to learn programming code.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a streak of excitement about finally moving off shop floor pay.
S1.quote: When the loader runs a full night shift with no one babysitting it, then I'll believe it.
S1.fieldNote: Adam's steadiness shows clearly: he'll retrain, but only after he's watched the robot work in his own cell. He sees steady change as a chance to get paid for work he already does. His worry is for Rui, an older operator who won't retrain, and he had no good answer for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's like, the next model year of tractors. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments now, not in five years. Pause on mass layoffs, income support for people who lose their jobs, tax the companies that replace whole factories. I'd post about it, which I never do, and I'd be at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the programming course doesn't save me in this one. If the AI writes the programs and robots load the machines, then Viktor's gone too, and he's got a master's degree. I'd be the cell lead of a cell that runs itself, for maybe a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything that isn't rent and food. Lina and I would cancel the holiday we've been saving for, which is about four hundred so far, and put it in the emergency pot. I'd go with the union to demand a redundancy deal with real money, and I'd look at whether my brother's moving company has room, even though robots will probably get there too. I'd register for whatever government support appears the first day it appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared. Not sleeping scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cancel the holiday. Where were you going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The coast, a cheap place her cousin has. We were going to get engaged there, actually. I haven't told her that. So it's not just a holiday, it's that, and that would have to wait too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning, is there anything you'd still try to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe how to repair the robots, the physical side, gearboxes and cables. Someone has to get covered in grease when they break. But I'd be guessing. Nobody can tell me which skill is safe in that world, and I don't have the money to guess twice.

S2.say: This needs governments now: a pause on mass layoffs, income support and taxes on companies that replace whole factories. I'd post about it, which I never do.
S2.think: The programming course doesn't save me, because if AI writes the programs then even the engineer with a master's degree is gone. I'd be lead of a cell that runs itself, for maybe a year.
S2.do: Cuts everything except rent and food and moves the 400 holiday fund into an emergency pot. Joins the union push for a real redundancy deal, asks about work at his brother's moving company and registers for government support as soon as it appears.
S2.feel: Proper scared, the kind that keeps him awake.
S2.quote: Nobody can tell me which skill is safe in that world, and I don't have the money to guess twice.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI takes away the move Adam was counting on, retraining into programming, and his thin savings mean he can't experiment. He quietly revealed he planned to propose to Lina on the holiday he'd cancel. His instinct shifts to collective and government action, which he normally leaves to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's something, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window and we should use it. Companies should be training people now, the government should be setting up support now, not after. I'd say it at work in plain words: start the courses this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd see it work somewhere else first, which is how I like it. Some factory in another country would have the AI cells first, and I'd watch. Then I'd know what's actually left for a person to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the programming course straight away, because even if it doesn't last forever it's more money for three or four years. I'd try to save a hundred a month from the raise. I'd still propose, because five years is long enough that I'm not putting my life on hold. And I'd get involved with the union's training committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but like I've got my hands on the wheel. Not like with the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still propose. With two years you'd wait. What's the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years it's a crash. You don't plan a wedding during a crash. With five years it's more like bad weather coming. You still live, you just keep a coat by the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be watching to know when it's getting close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Viktor. When the company stops sending him on courses and starts sending him to meetings about the new system, that's when. He's my early warning. He doesn't know that.

S3.say: We've got a window and we should use it. Companies and the government should be setting up training and support this year, not after.
S3.think: Five years means I'd see AI cells work somewhere else first, which is how I like it. Then I'd know what's actually left for a person to do.
S3.do: Starts the CNC programming course straight away for a few years of better pay and tries to save 100 a month from the raise. Joins the union's training committee and still plans to propose to Lina.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with his hands on the wheel, unlike the two-year picture.
S3.quote: You don't plan a wedding during a crash.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits Adam's style of watching others try something first. He treats the course as a bridge to a few better-paid years rather than a lifetime answer. The engagement goes ahead in this picture, which shows how much the warning time changes his personal plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Halfway through my working life, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same end point, so we'd better use the decade to decide who benefits. If machines do the work, people should get shorter weeks and a share of the profits, not just a pink slip. That's what I'd argue in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels almost normal. People change careers in ten years anyway. I'd have time to do the programming course, get a few good years from it, and then move again, maybe twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year I'd do the course and keep an eye on what the robot cells can do. Around year three or four I'd look at maintenance and repair, because I think fixing machines lasts longest. I'd try to get a small savings habit going, even fifty a month. And I'd vote for whoever has an actual plan, which I don't always bother doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a rattle in the spindle you can hear but can't find yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move twice. Doesn't that tire you out, just thinking about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. But my dad changed jobs four times, bus driver, warehouse, school caretaker. He never had a plan, he just went where there was work. At least I'd have warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be at Halden in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I'd like to be, I like the place. But Halden will be run from a laptop by then, maybe by one engineer for three cells. I'd want to be that engineer, but there'll only be one.

S4.say: It's the same end point, so we'd better use the decade to decide who benefits. People should get shorter weeks and a share of the profits, not just a pink slip.
S4.think: Ten years feels almost normal, because people change careers in ten years anyway. I'd get a few good years from programming and then move again, maybe twice.
S4.do: Does the programming course in the first year and plans to move into machine maintenance and repair by year three or four. Starts saving around 50 a month and votes for whichever party has a real plan.
S4.feel: Uneasy, like a rattle in the machine he can hear but can't find yet.
S4.quote: Halden will be run from a laptop by then, maybe by one engineer for three cells.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Adam's anxiety drops to a background rattle. He plans a staircase of moves, programming then maintenance, modelled on his father's many jobs. He still expects only one person to be left running several cells, and knows it might not be him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. My one plan, the programming course, stops working, and I can't afford to guess wrong. What would help is the company paying for training while I still have the job, and some income support that's in place before it all starts, not argued about afterwards.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to be good at something and still be poor. That's my whole situation already, before any robots. I'm the guy they call when the batch fails and I still borrowed from my brother for a deposit.

headlineQuote: I'm the guy they call when the batch fails and I still borrowed from my brother for a deposit.
portrait: Adam is a 27-year-old cell lead at a hydraulics plant, running four CNC machines and doing half the programmer's job on operator pay, with less than a month saved. He lives with Lina, a teaching assistant, and quietly plans to propose. He likes change once he's seen it work, so in the steady picture he'd retrain as a CNC programmer after watching the robot loader prove itself. Fast AGI takes that plan away and leaves him scared and turning to the union and government, while five or ten years let him plan a series of moves and keep his personal life on track.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his one plan of retraining as a programmer stops working and he can't afford to guess wrong.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid training while he still has the job, and income support set up before the change starts rather than argued about afterwards.
